checks.prompt: A speech pipeline receives whatever users upload: phone recordings in one container, screen recordings with a video track, podcast episodes in a lossy codec at various sample rates. Downstream, a recognition model wants exactly one shape, and a separate analysis step needs spectrograms. Which work belongs to this tool and which does not?
checks.explanation: The division is between changing the SHAPE of media and computing numbers FROM the samples. Containers, codecs, sample rates, channel counts, durations and track selection are this tool's domain, and it streams, so it handles files larger than memory. Spectrograms and other features are a signal-processing library's job — and in practice that library is often decoding through this same tool underneath, which is why they compose rather than compete.
options: This tool owns the transport and transform layer: demultiplexing containers, selecting and dropping streams, transcoding between codecs, resampling and remixing channels, trimming — turning any of those inputs into the one shape the model wants, streaming so file size is not bounded by memory. Computing spectrograms is not its job: numerical analysis of the samples belongs to a signal-processing library, which this tool usually feeds
Both belong to it: since it decodes to raw samples anyway, its filters are the natural place to compute spectral features, and using a separate library duplicates the decode
Neither: it is a media player and inspection utility, so a pipeline should decode with a signal-processing library and write files with it too
It owns the analysis and the library owns the conversion, because the library understands sample formats while this tool works only at the container level

checks.prompt: Describe the fixed left-to-right pipeline every invocation of this tool follows, naming each stage. Then explain the two distinctions the notebook says make everything click, and use the second one to explain why adding a single filter to an otherwise identical command can turn an instant, lossless operation into a slow and quality-destroying one. Finally state the rule for reading any command's option order.
checks.expected: A correct answer must lay out the pipeline: one or more inputs are demultiplexed and decoded to raw frames, those frames pass through a filtergraph, the results are encoded, and the encoded streams are multiplexed into one or more output containers. The first distinction is container versus stream: a container is a box holding one or more streams — video, one or more audio tracks, subtitles — and the tool demultiplexes the box on input and multiplexes streams back into a box on output, so choosing the output container and choosing each stream's codec are independent decisions. The second is copy versus re-encode: passing encoded packets straight through is a remux only — instant and lossless, but it cannot change the codec or apply any filter — whereas anything else decodes, filters and re-encodes. The consequence must be drawn precisely: adding a filter forces the decode-encode path, which is slower, and for a lossy codec each such round trip is generationally lossy, so quality degrades every time; that is why needless decode-encode round trips are worth avoiding. The order rule must be stated: read a command as global options, then the input flag and its file, then per-output options, then the output — options apply to the NEXT file, so those before an input configure that input and those after all inputs configure the next output. Noting that this is why a rate option placed before the input silently configures the input instead of the output is a plus.

checks.prompt: A recording has two audio tracks — a lapel microphone and a room microphone — plus video. A script that has always worked on single-track files now produces the wrong audio. Separately, the team wants a precise cut from a known timestamp and finds their extraction lands a fraction of a second early. Which pair of mechanisms explains and fixes these?
checks.explanation: Two unrelated mechanisms that both bite in real pipelines. Without explicit mapping the tool picks the stream it considers best, which is fine until there is more than one candidate — so be explicit about which track flows to the output, and use the drop-video or drop-audio flags when you want a whole type gone. And seek placement is a genuine trade: before the input is a fast keyframe seek that can land slightly off; after the input it decodes from the start and is sample-accurate, which is what a precise audio trim needs.
options: With several candidate streams the tool auto-selects what it judges best, which is not necessarily the one meant — explicit stream mapping selects the exact track, and there are also flags to drop video or audio wholesale. The early landing is seek placement: putting the start time before the input performs a fast seek to the nearest keyframe, while putting it after the input decodes from the beginning and cuts exactly, at the cost of speed
Multiple audio tracks are always merged into one, so the fix is to split them afterwards; and the imprecise cut means the duration option was used instead of an end timestamp
The wrong track is chosen because tracks are ordered by bitrate, so re-encoding the file at a uniform bitrate fixes the ordering; the imprecise cut is a rounding artefact of the output sample rate
Both come from stream copying: copying preserves the original track order and keyframe layout, so re-encoding without copying resolves the track selection and the seek accuracy together

checks.prompt: Model the command grammar in Python — no binary is invoked. Define `PCM_CODECS`, `LOSSY_CODECS` and a `CONTAINER_CODECS` mapping at least `".wav"` to the PCM codecs, `".flac"` to `{"flac"}`, `".mp3"` to `{"libmp3lame"}`, `".m4a"` to `{"aac"}` and `".opus"` to `{"libopus"}`. Write `ffmpeg_command(source, output, *, sample_rate=None, channels=None, codec=None, filters=(), copy=False, start=None, duration=None, fast_seek=False, drop_video=False, overwrite=True)` returning the argument list. Raise `ValueError` if `copy` is combined with any of `filters`, `codec`, `sample_rate` or `channels`, and raise `ValueError` if `codec` is given and the output's extension is a KNOWN key of the mapping that does not list it (an unknown extension is accepted). Otherwise build, in order: `"ffmpeg"`, then `"-y"` or `"-n"`, then `"-loglevel", "error"`; then `"-ss", str(start)` if a start was given AND `fast_seek`; then `"-i", source`; then `"-ss", str(start)` if a start was given and NOT `fast_seek`; then `"-t", str(duration)` if given; then `"-vn"` if dropping video; then `"-c", "copy"` if copying; then `"-af"` with the filters joined by commas if any; then `"-ar"`, `"-ac"` and `"-c:a"` for whichever were given; then `output`. Write `explain(argv)` reading such a list back: walk the tokens after the program name, treating `"-y"`, `"-n"`, `"-vn"`, `"-an"`, `"-shortest"` and `"-nostats"` as flags with the value True and any other token starting with `"-"` as taking the next token as its value; each `"-i"` records its file in `inputs` and everything AFTER the first input belongs to the output rather than the input. Return `{"inputs", "output", "input_options", "output_options", "reencodes"}`, where `output` is the last bare token, and `reencodes` is True only when the output options do NOT set copying and DO contain at least one of `-ar`, `-ac`, `-af`, `-vf`, `-c:a` or `-c:v`. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Every assertion here is a mistake somebody makes with the real tool. The two seek commands differ only in where one option sits, and that placement is the entire difference between a fast approximate cut and a slow exact one. The refusals encode a contradiction rather than a preference: passing packets through untouched cannot also filter or re-encode them, and a container can only hold codecs it knows how to carry — asking for both is a command that cannot mean anything. And the pair of read-back cases at the end is the classic silent failure: the identical rate option one position to the left configures the INPUT, so nothing is resampled, no error is raised, and the file is simply wrong. Note also what re-encoding is judged by: it is not whether the container changed, it is whether anything asked the samples to be decoded and written again.
checks.test:
# The canonical preprocessing command, in the order the grammar requires.
assert ffmpeg_command("in.mp4", "out.wav", sample_rate=16000, channels=1,
                      codec="pcm_s16le") == [
    "ffmpeg", "-y", "-loglevel", "error", "-i", "in.mp4",
    "-ar", "16000", "-ac", "1", "-c:a", "pcm_s16le", "out.wav"]

# Automation never prompts: overwrite is explicit either way.
assert ffmpeg_command("a.wav", "b.wav", overwrite=False)[1] == "-n"
assert "-y" in ffmpeg_command("a.wav", "b.wav")

# Seek placement is the whole difference between fast and accurate: BEFORE the
# input is a keyframe seek, AFTER it decodes from the start and lands exactly.
fast = ffmpeg_command("in.mp4", "out.wav", start=30, duration=5, fast_seek=True)
assert fast.index("-ss") < fast.index("-i"), fast
assert fast[fast.index("-ss") + 1] == "30"
accurate = ffmpeg_command("in.mp4", "out.wav", start=30, duration=5)
assert accurate.index("-ss") > accurate.index("-i"), accurate
assert accurate.index("-t") > accurate.index("-i"), accurate
assert accurate[accurate.index("-t") + 1] == "5"

# Filters chain in declaration order, comma separated, in one audio filter option.
built = ffmpeg_command("clip.mp4", "out.wav", drop_video=True,
                       filters=["atrim=0:1", "volume=0.5"], sample_rate=16000,
                       channels=1)
assert "-vn" in built and built.index("-vn") > built.index("-i")
assert built[built.index("-af") + 1] == "atrim=0:1,volume=0.5", built

# Passing packets through untouched is remux ONLY: asking for a filter or any
# re-encoding alongside it is a contradiction, not a silent fallback.
assert ffmpeg_command("in.mkv", "out.mp4", copy=True) == [
    "ffmpeg", "-y", "-loglevel", "error", "-i", "in.mkv", "-c", "copy", "out.mp4"]
for kwargs in ({"filters": ["volume=0.5"]}, {"sample_rate": 16000},
               {"channels": 1}, {"codec": "aac"}):
    try:
        ffmpeg_command("in.mkv", "out.mp4", copy=True, **kwargs)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"copy with {kwargs} must be refused")

# The container and the codec are separate decisions, but not independent ones.
for bad in [("out.mp3", "pcm_s16le"), ("out.wav", "aac"), ("out.wav", "libmp3lame"),
            ("out.m4a", "libopus")]:
    try:
        ffmpeg_command("in.wav", bad[0], codec=bad[1])
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")
for good in [("out.wav", "pcm_s16le"), ("out.mp3", "libmp3lame"),
             ("out.m4a", "aac"), ("out.flac", "flac")]:
    ffmpeg_command("in.wav", good[0], codec=good[1])
# An unknown extension is not second-guessed.
ffmpeg_command("in.wav", "out.weird", codec="pcm_s16le")

# Reading a command back: everything before the input configures the INPUT.
right = explain(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", "in.wav", "-ar", "16000", "out.wav"])
assert right["inputs"] == ["in.wav"] and right["output"] == "out.wav"
assert right["output_options"]["-ar"] == "16000", right
assert "-ar" not in right["input_options"], right
assert right["reencodes"] is True

# ...which is exactly why the same options moved one place to the left mean
# something entirely different, and quietly do not do what was intended.
wrong = explain(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-ar", "16000", "-i", "in.wav", "out.wav"])
assert wrong["input_options"]["-ar"] == "16000", wrong
assert wrong["output_options"] == {}, wrong
assert wrong["reencodes"] is False, wrong

# Passing packets straight through is recognised as not re-encoding, even though
# the container changes.
remux = explain(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", "in.mkv", "-c", "copy", "out.mp4"])
assert remux["reencodes"] is False and remux["output"] == "out.mp4"
assert explain(["ffmpeg", "-i", "in.mkv", "-c", "copy", "-af", "volume=0.5",
                "out.mp4"])["reencodes"] is False

# Flags that take no value are not mistaken for options that do.
flags = explain(["ffmpeg", "-y", "-i", "clip.mp4", "-vn", "-ac", "1", "out.wav"])
assert flags["output_options"]["-vn"] is True, flags
assert flags["output_options"]["-ac"] == "1", flags
assert flags["output"] == "out.wav", flags

# Several inputs are all recorded, and options after the last one are the output's.
several = explain(["ffmpeg", "-f", "lavfi", "-i", "testsrc=duration=2",
                   "-f", "lavfi", "-i", "sine=frequency=330", "-shortest", "out.mp4"])
assert several["inputs"] == ["testsrc=duration=2", "sine=frequency=330"], several
assert several["output"] == "out.mp4", several

# Round trip: what the builder produces reads back as the output options it set.
back = explain(ffmpeg_command("in.mp4", "out.wav", sample_rate=16000, channels=1,
                              codec="pcm_s16le"))
assert back["output_options"] == {"-ar": "16000", "-ac": "1", "-c:a": "pcm_s16le"}, back
assert back["reencodes"] is True

checks.prompt: A batch job in continuous integration hangs on some files with no output and no error, and the team cannot find any log lines from the tool in the captured standard output. A colleague suggests the tool is crashing silently. What is actually happening?
checks.explanation: Two of the most common automation traps, and they compound each other. The prompt before overwriting an existing file blocks on standard input, which in a non-interactive job is indistinguishable from a hang — so scripts should always state the overwrite policy explicitly. And the diagnostics go to standard error by design, because standard output is reserved for media being piped out; a harness capturing only standard output therefore sees silence, which makes the first problem much harder to diagnose.
options: Two things, and neither is a crash. Without an explicit overwrite decision the tool prompts before replacing an existing output and blocks waiting on standard input, which in an unattended job looks exactly like a hang — always pass the overwrite or the never-overwrite flag. And its progress and diagnostic output goes to standard ERROR, not standard output, which is reserved for piped media, so capturing only standard output finds nothing; capture standard error, and quiet the banner with a log-level option or ask for machine-readable progress
The hang is caused by files larger than memory, which the tool buffers before writing; the missing logs confirm it, since logging starts only after the buffer is flushed
The tool writes logs to standard output but only when attached to a terminal, so in continuous integration they are suppressed; the hang is an unrelated network timeout while probing codecs
Both symptoms mean the output container was not specified, so the tool waits for the format to be chosen interactively and suppresses logging until it is

checks.prompt: A team is standardising their audio preprocessing. Options on the table: shell out to this tool directly; use a Python wrapper that builds its argument list; use a convenience library for slicing and concatenating clips; or use a signal-processing library for everything. Give the trade-off for each and recommend an approach for a pipeline that ingests user uploads of unpredictable format and size and must produce one canonical shape. Then state the rule of thumb that decides which tool a media task belongs to.
checks.expected: A correct answer must weigh all four. Shelling out directly is the durable skill and the most capable option — it covers every conversion, transcode, resample, trim, multiplex and extraction — with the honest cost that it is a command-line grammar that is dense and easy to get subtly wrong, and that errors arrive as text on standard error. A wrapper that builds the argument list is convenient for expressing complex filtergraphs as a graph in Python, but it is still the same binary underneath, so it adds a dependency and can obscure the underlying error. A convenience library for slicing and concatenating short clips is pleasant for simple in-Python edits, but it loads audio into memory, is awkward for large files or video, and typically calls the same binary anyway. A signal-processing library analyses samples — spectrograms, features — and does not transcode containers and codecs at all, and its own input backend is frequently this tool. The recommendation must follow from the stated constraints: unpredictable formats and unbounded sizes mean shelling out to the binary, because it streams rather than loading into memory and handles the full matrix of containers and codecs, forcing the sample rate, channel count and sample format explicitly rather than trusting the source. The rule of thumb must be stated: if the task changes the shape or format of media it belongs to this tool, and if it computes numbers from the samples it belongs to the analysis library — which this tool then feeds. Noting that a graphical editor is fine for one-off manual work but is not reproducible in a pipeline, or that managed cloud transcoding is for scale rather than local preprocessing, is a plus.
